title: Would we treat a chatbot error the way we'd treat a human agent's error?
description: A board-level oversight question testing whether an organization has actually extended its existing accountability and correction processes to AI chatbot output, rather than assuming a chatbot's statements carry less liability than a human agent's.

history.note: Normalized US/UK spelling variants to the American-English house style (schema field names, e.g. organizations_involved, are already American; majority framework citations - NIST, FTC, EEOC, FCRA, BIPA - are American sources).

question_text: If our customer-facing AI chatbot gives a customer incorrect information about pricing, eligibility, or policy, have we assessed our legal liability exposure the same way we would for a human agent's documented error — and would that liability hold up if challenged, as Air Canada's disclaimer argument did not?
rationale: Moffatt v. Air Canada shows that a 'the chatbot is a separate entity' defence does not hold up in practice. Boards should confirm their own organization is not relying on an equivalent, untested assumption.
follow_up_actions: Confirm chatbot responses to policy-sensitive questions are grounded in current source-of-truth policy documents.
Confirm there is a review/correction process for chatbot errors comparable to the process for human agent errors.
Ask legal/compliance whether the organization's terms of service attempt to disclaim chatbot statements, and whether that disclaimer has been tested.

citations.title: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149
citations.publisher: Civil Resolution Tribunal of British Columbia
